item.title: Guns, Faith, and Climate: What's at Stake as the Supreme Court Opens a Blockbuster New Term
item.body:
## A Term Packed With High-Stakes Questions

The U.S. Supreme Court is set to open its new annual term on October 5, and the docket already includes roughly 20 cases touching on some of the most contested legal questions in American life. Among the issues justices are expected to weigh: the constitutionality of state bans on certain semi-automatic weapons, whether religious schools can participate in state-funded preschool programs, and whether oil and gas companies can be held liable in state courts for their role in climate change.

Legal observers say the combination of cases gives this term the potential to reshape how courts, states, and industries operate for years to come. Here's a plain-language look at what each dispute involves and why it matters.

## Assault-Style Weapons Bans

Several states have enacted restrictions on semi-automatic rifles often described as "assault-style weapons," arguing the measures reduce mass-casualty risks. Gun rights advocates counter that such bans conflict with Second Amendment protections as interpreted in recent Supreme Court precedent, which has told lower courts to evaluate modern firearm laws against historical traditions of regulation.

A ruling either way would carry major consequences. A decision striking down state bans could invalidate similar laws in multiple states. A decision upholding them could give legislatures more room to regulate firearm types without running afoul of the Constitution. Either outcome is likely to intensify an already active public debate, so most legal analysts expect the Court to issue a narrowly tailored opinion focused on the specific laws before it rather than a sweeping national rule.

## Religious Schools and Public Preschool Funding

A separate set of cases asks whether states that fund preschool or early-childhood education programs can exclude religious schools from participating solely because of their religious character. The Court has ruled in recent years that states generally cannot deny public benefits to religious institutions simply for being religious, while still permitting some restrictions tied to how funds are actually used.

This term's cases could clarify where that line falls for early education specifically. Supporters of including faith-based schools argue that excluding them amounts to discrimination against religion. Opponents, including some public education advocates, argue that a ruling requiring inclusion could raise church-state separation concerns and complicate oversight of curriculum and staffing standards in publicly funded classrooms. Whatever the Court decides, it will likely be closely studied by school choice programs nationwide.

## Oil Companies and Climate Liability

Perhaps the most closely watched business case involves whether states and municipalities can sue energy companies in state court for damages tied to climate change, such as the cost of coastal flooding or infrastructure repair. Energy companies argue these claims belong in federal court, or that they are effectively regulated by federal climate and environmental law, not state tort law. Plaintiff cities and states argue they are entitled to pursue traditional damages claims, similar to past lawsuits against other industries, through the state court system.

A ruling permitting these suits to proceed in state courts could open the door to a wave of new litigation with potentially significant financial exposure for the energy sector. A ruling limiting them to federal jurisdiction, where courts have so far been more skeptical of these theories, could effectively close off one of the most active legal strategies climate advocates have pursued in the past decade.

## Why This Term Stands Out

Individually, each of these disputes would be significant. Together, they place the Court at the center of debates over public safety, religious liberty, and environmental accountability all within a single term. Because the justices tend to move cautiously on issues with broad social and economic ripple effects, most rulings are not expected until spring or early summer of next year.

In the meantime, legal experts, industry groups, and advocacy organizations on all sides are expected to closely track oral arguments for early signals about how the Court may lean. As always, the eventual opinions will likely turn on narrow legal reasoning specific to each case rather than broad political statements, even as the practical stakes extend well beyond the courtroom.
